theory.question: When does a single-node database stop being enough and you need sharding — with concrete capacity numbers for PostgreSQL, MongoDB, Redis, and DynamoDB
theory.answer:
Shard when data volume or write throughput exceeds what one node can store or process; if reads are the bottleneck, replication alone may suffice.

PostgreSQL (single node, no external sharding layer):
- Storage ceiling on managed Postgres is large but finite — AWS RDS PostgreSQL supports up to 64 TiB per instance; io2 storage can reach 256,000 provisioned IOPS and up to 16,000 MiB/s throughput on the largest configurations.
- Practical trigger is earlier: when the working set no longer fits RAM, write-heavy traffic saturates CPU/WAL/disk IOPS, or maintenance (vacuum, index builds, backups) becomes operationally risky. Vanilla PostgreSQL has no built-in horizontal sharding — you add Citus, Vitess, or application-level sharding when vertical scaling stops helping.

MongoDB (replica set → sharded cluster):
- MongoDB guidance: plan sharding when a collection approaches ~2–3 TB, or when a large instance (e.g., Atlas M60 with 4 TB disk) sits at 60–70% CPU/RAM/storage utilization for sustained periods.
- High sustained write throughput on a single primary is another signal — the same capacity rule applies: one leader can become the bottleneck even if total cluster storage is fine.

Redis (in-memory, cluster sharding):
- Data must fit in RAM on the nodes serving it (unless using tiered/flash extensions). Set `maxmemory` to ~70–80% of host RAM — e.g., ~22–26 GB on a 32 GB host, ~45–51 GB on 64 GB, ~90–102 GB on 128 GB; AWS ElastiCache's largest single node (cache.r7g.16xlarge) offers up to 512 GiB.
- A single open-source Redis process is single-threaded for commands — typical throughput is on the order of tens of thousands to low hundreds of thousands of ops/sec depending on value size and pipelining; Redis Enterprise benchmarks show ~5M ops/sec per large node with many shards. Shard when one node's memory (often before a ~64–128 GB working set on OSS Redis) or command throughput is saturated.

Cross-cutting book thresholds useful in design reviews:
- HBase auto-splits a region at ~10 GB by default, or when write throughput stays above a configured threshold.
- Fixed-shard designs (Citus, Riak, Elasticsearch) often pre-create hundreds or thousands of logical shards — e.g., 1,000 shards on 10 nodes (100 per node) — so node add/remove moves whole shards, not individual keys.

Sources: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonRDS/latest/UserGuide/CHAP_Storage.html , https://www.mongodb.com/resources/products/capabilities/sharding , https://redis.io/docs/latest/operate/rs/databases/memory-performance/ , https://docs.aws.amazon.com/amazondynamodb/latest/developerguide/bp-partition-key-design.html

theory.question: Pros and cons of using sharding for multitenant SaaS (one shard per tenant vs several tenants per shard)
theory.answer:
Multitenant sharding trades operational isolation and compliance convenience against overhead and cross-tenant feature cost.

A SaaS tenant is a naturally separate dataset, such as one business in an email-marketing service. A large tenant can receive a dedicated shard while several small tenants share one shard.

Recommendation pattern: shard-by-tenant for large enterprise customers with strict isolation/residency needs; pool small tenants on shared shards with a tenant ID in every partition key; plan tenant migration tooling early.

Comment: AWS cell-based architecture whitepaper and Citus schema-based sharding are production implementations of this model.

theory.question: Key-range sharding: how it works, when to choose it, and how rebalancing happens
theory.answer:
Key-range sharding assigns each shard a contiguous interval of partition keys — like encyclopedia volumes sorted by title.

Boundaries may be manual (Vitess) or automatic (Bigtable/HBase, MongoDB range sharding, CockroachDB, FoundationDB). Ranges are not necessarily equal width — volume 12 may cover T–Z — so boundaries adapt to keep shards roughly even.

Choose key-range when:
- You need range queries on the partition key (time-series, lexicographic browsing).
- You can structure the key so related reads cluster without creating write hot spots (prefix sensor ID before timestamp).

Comment: Monotonic timestamp keys are a classic footgun — App Engine and HBase documentation describes the same risk.

theory.question: Hash-modulo sharding (`hash(key) % N`): mechanism and why changing node count is painful
theory.answer:
Hash-modulo sharding computes `hash(key) % N` and sends the key to that numbered shard. It is simple, deterministic, and usually spreads well-behaved keys evenly when the hash function is stable.

The problem is that `N` participates in every placement decision. Changing from eight shards to nine changes the remainder for most hashes, so most records move even though capacity increased by only one ninth. During that migration, clients need a transition map, dual reads or writes, and a way to reconcile requests that race with movement. A partial rollout can otherwise lose or duplicate data.

Use modulo only when the logical shard count is fixed and physical nodes can own several logical shards. If the number of placement buckets itself must grow, prefer consistent hashing, rendezvous hashing, or dynamically split hash ranges so membership changes move only a bounded share of keys.

theory.question: Fixed number of logical shards (many shards, fewer nodes): how it works and its limits
theory.answer:
Create many logical shards up front, then assign several of them to each physical node. Routing has two steps: hash the key to a logical shard, then look up which node currently owns that shard. Adding capacity moves whole logical shards and updates only the ownership map; records keep the same logical-shard identity.

This makes rebalancing predictable and supports heterogeneous machines by assigning more shards to stronger nodes. It also keeps the logical shard count stable while the node count changes.

The main limitation is that the initial shard count is a long-lived capacity decision. Too few shards cap future parallelism and make each move large; too many increase metadata, file, connection, and coordination overhead. A single hot key also remains hot because a logical shard cannot divide one key. Elasticsearch, Citus, Riak, and Couchbase use variants of this pattern.

theory.question: Hash-range sharding: combine hashing with dynamic range splits
theory.answer:
Hash-range sharding assigns each shard a contiguous range of hash values, not raw keys — getting even spread without fixing shard count upfront.

Downside vs raw key-range: range queries on the partition key scatter across all shards. Exception: composite keys where only the first column is the partition key — range queries on later columns stay within one shard if the prefix is fixed.

YugabyteDB, DynamoDB, and MongoDB offer hash-range style sharding.

Comment: This is the default mental model for DynamoDB — partition key hash determines the partition; sort key gives ordering inside the partition.

theory.question: Consistent hashing: properties and tradeoffs vs range splits
theory.answer:
Consistent hashing places both keys and shard owners in a hash space so a membership change remaps only the affected portion of that space. Virtual nodes or multiple tokens per owner improve balance; rendezvous and jump hashing provide related placement properties without maintaining the same ring structure.

The benefit is limited data movement when nodes join or leave. The costs are more complex routing, uneven ownership without enough tokens, and weaker locality for bulk transfer when a new owner receives scattered ranges.

Dynamic hash-range splitting is often easier for storage engines: each shard owns a contiguous interval of hash values, and an overloaded interval can split into two adjacent intervals. Consistent or rendezvous placement is attractive for caches and stateless routing; explicit ranges are attractive when operators need inspectable boundaries, streaming migration, and range-level metadata.

theory.question: Hot key / hot shard problem: causes and mitigation techniques
theory.answer:
A hot shard receives much more traffic than its peers; a hot key concentrates that traffic on one partition even when the overall key distribution is balanced.

Common causes include monotonically increasing range keys, celebrity accounts, viral posts, a small set of popular products, and low-cardinality secondary-index values. Measure requests, bytes, CPU, queue depth, and tail latency per shard and per key; cluster-wide averages hide the hotspot.

Mitigations depend on the access pattern. Add a nonmonotonic prefix to time-series keys, split one logical counter across suffix buckets, cache popular reads, replicate read-only hot data, rate-limit abusive clients, or isolate exceptional tenants. Splitting writes makes reads fan out and merge, so it should be targeted and reversible. Rebalancing an already saturated shard can add enough network and disk work to worsen the incident, which is why emergency moves need throttling and careful control.

theory.question:
Request routing to shards: three approaches, coordination with ZooKeeper/etcd, and solutions to shared hard problems:
- Who decides shard→node mapping, and how is the coordinator fault-tolerant without split brain?
- How do routers learn mapping changes?
- During shard migration, requests may still be in flight to the old node — need cutover handling.
theory.answer:
Request routing answers: given a key, which IP:port owns its shard?

Three approaches:
1. Contact any node (round-robin LB) — owner serves locally; otherwise forwards to the right node and relays the reply.
2. Dedicated routing tier (e.g., MongoDB `mongos`) — shard-aware load balancer that does not store data.
3. Shard-aware clients — connect directly to the correct node with no proxy.

Coordinator fault tolerance (who decides mapping, avoiding split brain):
- A small control plane holds the authoritative shard→node map — not individual data nodes and not DNS. Operators or an auto-rebalancer propose moves; only the coordinator commits them.
- The coordinator itself runs as a replicated quorum service (ZooKeeper ZAB, etcd Raft, MongoDB config-server replica set). Writes need a majority of replicas to ack, so a partitioned minority cannot publish a conflicting map — that is how split brain is avoided.
- Single-writer semantics: one elected leader applies mapping changes; followers replicate the log. Clients and routers read from any healthy replica but mutations go through the leader.
- Fencing with monotonic epochs: every mapping update carries a version/generation number (ZK zxid, etcd revision, MongoDB config version). Data nodes and routers reject or ignore assignments from a stale epoch — a zombie leader that lost quorum cannot overwrite a newer map.
- Data nodes register liveness (ephemeral ZK nodes, lease heartbeats). If a node is declared dead, the coordinator reassigns its shards only after the lease expires — avoids two nodes believing they own the same shard.
- Built-in Raft on data nodes (Kafka controller, YugabyteDB/TiDB placement driver, ScyllaDB) follows the same quorum rules without a separate ZK cluster.
- Riak gossip alternative: peers exchange mapping state without a central coordinator — simpler ops, weaker guarantees, possible divergent views tolerated because Riak already offers eventual consistency.

Comment: Vitess VTGate is another routing-tier example for MySQL sharding.

theory.question: Local vs global secondary indexes on a sharded database — write path, read path, and when to pick each
theory.answer:
A local secondary index is partitioned exactly like the primary table. Updating one row changes only its primary shard and that shard's index, so writes stay local. A query by the secondary attribute must contact every shard and combine the results because matching entries may exist anywhere.

A global secondary index is partitioned by the indexed value. The query can route directly to the relevant index shard, but a base-row write may update a different machine, creating distributed write amplification and a consistency problem between the table and index.

Choose local indexes for write-heavy OLTP when secondary queries are rare, narrow, or tolerant of scatter-gather. Choose global indexes when indexed lookups dominate and low read latency justifies the extra write path. For broad search and ranking, a separate search tier fed from the system of record is often clearer than adding many globally maintained indexes.

theory.question: Automatic vs manual shard rebalancing — tradeoffs and when a human should stay in the loop
theory.answer:
Automatic rebalancing reacts quickly and reduces routine operator work, but a controller can mistake temporary load, a slow dependency, or a partial outage for a permanent capacity change. Moving data consumes the same disk and network resources already under pressure, so an aggressive feedback loop can amplify the incident.

Manual rebalancing gives an operator context and control but responds slowly and is prone to inconsistent procedures. A hybrid is usually safer: the control plane computes a proposed assignment, estimates bytes and load, and requires approval for risky moves while allowing tightly bounded repairs automatically.

Throttle transfer bandwidth, limit concurrent moves, monitor replication lag and tail latency, and make ownership changes atomic. During a move, define how in-flight reads and writes reach the old and new owners. Disable or dampen automatic movement during known overload, then resume it after the cluster has spare capacity.

practice.task: [Python, SQLite] Learn how to compare local and catalog secondary indexes across application-level shards.
practice.question:
This exercise uses real on-disk SQLite databases through Python's standard-library `sqlite3` module. Three database files act as application-level primary shards, while a fourth SQLite database is an application-maintained catalog. You will compare a scatter/gather query over native local indexes with a catalog lookup that routes primary-key fetches. SQLite does not synchronize the catalog automatically; the application must maintain it.

Prerequisites: Python 3.10+ (stdlib only; no pip packages required).

Setup:

```bash
mkdir sqlite-shard-lab
cd sqlite-shard-lab
python3 --version
```

Save the starter file below as `sqlite_shard_indexes.py`.

from __future__ import annotations

from pathlib import Path

DATA_DIR = Path("car_shards")
SHARD_PATHS = [DATA_DIR / f"shard_{number}.db" for number in range(3)]
CATALOG_PATH = DATA_DIR / "catalog.db"
COLOR_QUERY = """
SELECT listing_id
FROM listings
WHERE color = ? AND price < ?
ORDER BY listing_id
"""
CATALOG_QUERY = """
SELECT listing_id, shard_id
FROM listing_directory
WHERE color = ? AND price < ?
ORDER BY listing_id
"""
ROWS = [
    (100, "Honda", "blue", 9000, "Dallas"),
    (250, "Toyota", "red", 14000, "Austin"),
    (401, "Ford", "red", 8000, "Houston"),
    (520, "Toyota", "silver", 16000, "Austin"),
    (742, "Toyota", "red", 12000, "Austin"),
    (803, "BMW", "black", 22000, "Austin"),
    (910, "Toyota", "red", 14999, "Dallas"),
    (999, "Honda", "red", 15500, "Austin"),
]


def shard_for(listing_id: int) -> int:
    return listing_id % len(SHARD_PATHS)


def reset_databases() -> None:
    DATA_DIR.mkdir(exist_ok=True)
    for path in [*SHARD_PATHS, CATALOG_PATH]:
        path.unlink(missing_ok=True)

    for path in SHARD_PATHS:
        with sqlite3.connect(path) as db:
            db.execute("PRAGMA journal_mode=DELETE")
            db.execute(
                """
                CREATE TABLE listings (
                    listing_id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
                    make TEXT NOT NULL,
                    color TEXT NOT NULL,
                    price INTEGER NOT NULL,
                    city TEXT NOT NULL

    reset_databases()
    create_local_indexes()
    rebuild_catalog()

    local = query_local("red", 15000)
    catalog = query_catalog("red", 15000)
    expected_ids = [250, 401, 742, 910]

    assert local["listing_ids"] == expected_ids
    assert catalog["listing_ids"] == expected_ids
    assert local["queried_shards"] == [0, 1, 2]
    assert catalog["fetched_shards"] == [1, 2]

Each function returns the basenames of the database files it wrote.

6. Run the assertions:

            )
            """
        )
        for shard_id, path in enumerate(SHARD_PATHS):
            with sqlite3.connect(path) as shard_db:
                rows = shard_db.execute(
                    "SELECT listing_id, color, price FROM listings"
                )
                catalog_db.executemany(
                    "INSERT INTO listing_directory "
                    "(listing_id, shard_id, color, price) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?)",
                    ((listing_id, shard_id, color, price) for listing_id, color, price in rows),
                )
        catalog_db.execute(
            "CREATE INDEX idx_directory_color_price "
            "ON listing_directory(color, price)"
        )


def query_local(color: str, price_cap: int) -> dict[str, object]:
    listing_ids: list[int] = []
    plans: list[list[str]] = []
    parameters = (color, price_cap)
    for path in SHARD_PATHS:
        with sqlite3.connect(path) as db:
            plans.append(explain(db, COLOR_QUERY, parameters))
            listing_ids.extend(row[0] for row in db.execute(COLOR_QUERY, parameters))
    return {
        "listing_ids": sorted(listing_ids),
        "queried_shards": list(range(len(SHARD_PATHS))),
        "plans": plans,
    }


def query_catalog(color: str, price_cap: int) -> dict[str, object]:
    parameters = (color, price_cap)
    with sqlite3.connect(CATALOG_PATH) as catalog_db:
        catalog_plan = explain(catalog_db, CATALOG_QUERY, parameters)
        routing_rows = list(catalog_db.execute(CATALOG_QUERY, parameters))

    ids_by_shard: dict[int, list[int]] = {}
    for listing_id, shard_id in routing_rows:
        ids_by_shard.setdefault(shard_id, []).append(listing_id)

    fetched_ids: list[int] = []
    for shard_id, listing_ids in ids_by_shard.items():
        with sqlite3.connect(SHARD_PATHS[shard_id]) as shard_db:
            for listing_id in listing_ids:
                row = shard_db.execute(
                    "SELECT listing_id FROM listings WHERE listing_id = ?", (listing_id,)
                ).fetchone()
                if row is not None:
                    fetched_ids.append(row[0])
    return {
        "listing_ids": sorted(fetched_ids),
        "fetched_shards": sorted(ids_by_shard),
        "catalog_plan": catalog_plan,
    }


def update_local(listing_id: int, new_price: int) -> list[str]:
    path = SHARD_PATHS[shard_for(listing_id)]
    with sqlite3.connect(path) as db:
        db.execute(
            "UPDATE listings SET price = ? WHERE listing_id = ?",
            (new_price, listing_id),
        )
    return [path.name]


def update_with_catalog(listing_id: int, new_price: int) -> list[str]:
    shard_path = SHARD_PATHS[shard_for(listing_id)]
    with sqlite3.connect(shard_path) as db:
        db.execute("ATTACH DATABASE ? AS catalog", (str(CATALOG_PATH),))
        try:
            with db:
                db.execute(
                    "UPDATE main.listings SET price = ? WHERE listing_id = ?",
                    (new_price, listing_id),
                )
                db.execute(
                    "UPDATE catalog.listing_directory SET price = ? WHERE listing_id = ?",
                    (new_price, listing_id),
                )
        finally:
            db.execute("DETACH DATABASE catalog")
    return [shard_path.name, CATALOG_PATH.name]


def verify() -> None:
    reset_databases()
    create_local_indexes()
    rebuild_catalog()

    local = query_local("red", 15000)
    catalog = query_catalog("red", 15000)
    expected_ids = [250, 401, 742, 910]

    assert local["listing_ids"] == expected_ids
    assert catalog["listing_ids"] == expected_ids
    assert local["queried_shards"] == [0, 1, 2]
    assert catalog["fetched_shards"] == [1, 2]
    assert all(
        any("idx_listings_color_price" in detail for detail in plan)
        for plan in local["plans"]
    )
    assert any(
        "idx_directory_color_price" in detail
        for detail in catalog["catalog_plan"]
    )

    assert update_local(742, 11000) == ["shard_1.db"]

    reset_databases()
    create_local_indexes()
    rebuild_catalog()
    assert set(update_with_catalog(742, 11000)) == {
        "catalog.db",
        "shard_1.db",
    }
    with sqlite3.connect(SHARD_PATHS[1]) as shard_db:
        primary_price = shard_db.execute(
            "SELECT price FROM listings WHERE listing_id = 742"
        ).fetchone()[0]
    with sqlite3.connect(CATALOG_PATH) as catalog_db:
        catalog_price = catalog_db.execute(
            "SELECT price FROM listing_directory WHERE listing_id = 742"
        ).fetchone()[0]
    assert primary_price == catalog_price == 11000

    print("local_plan=", local["plans"])
    print("catalog_plan=", catalog["catalog_plan"])
    print("verification=passed")


if __name__ == "__main__":
    verify()
```

```python
#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Consistent-hashing ring with virtual-node rebalance plans."""
from __future__ import annotations

import bisect
import hashlib
from collections import defaultdict
from dataclasses import dataclass, field

KEYS = [f"key-{i:05d}" for i in range(10_000)]
VNODE_COUNT = 128
NODES_3 = ["node-a", "node-b", "node-c"]
NODES_4 = NODES_3 + ["node-d"]


def stable_hash(key: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode()).hexdigest(), 16)


@dataclass
class HashRing:
    vnode_count: int = VNODE_COUNT
    _positions: list[int] = field(default_factory=list)
    _owners: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)
    _key_cache: dict[str, str] = field(default_factory=dict)

    def _insert_vnodes(self, node: str) -> None:
        for i in range(self.vnode_count):
            position = stable_hash(f"{node}#{i}")
            index = bisect.bisect_right(self._positions, position)
            self._positions.insert(index, position)
            self._owners.insert(index, node)

    def _remove_vnodes(self, node: str) -> None:
        retained = [
            (position, owner)
            for position, owner in zip(self._positions, self._owners)
            if owner != node
        ]
        self._positions = [position for position, _ in retained]
        self._owners = [owner for _, owner in retained]

    def build(self, nodes: list[str]) -> None:
        self._positions.clear()
        self._owners.clear()
        self._key_cache.clear()
        for node in nodes:
            self._insert_vnodes(node)

    def get_node(self, key: str) -> str:
        if key in self._key_cache:
            return self._key_cache[key]
        if not self._positions:
            raise ValueError("cannot look up a key on an empty ring")

        index = bisect.bisect_left(self._positions, stable_hash(key))
        if index == len(self._positions):
            index = 0
        owner = self._owners[index]
        self._key_cache[key] = owner
        return owner

    def _diff(self, keys: list[str], before: dict[str, str]) -> list[dict]:
        migrations = []
        for key in keys:
            destination = self.get_node(key)
            source = before[key]
            if source != destination:
                migrations.append({"key": key, "from": source, "to": destination})
        return migrations

    def add_node(self, node: str, keys: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
        before = {key: self.get_node(key) for key in keys}
        self._insert_vnodes(node)
        self._key_cache.clear()
        return self._diff(keys, before)

    def remove_node(self, node: str, keys: list[str]) -> list[dict]:
        before = {key: self.get_node(key) for key in keys}
        self._remove_vnodes(node)
        self._key_cache.clear()
        return self._diff(keys, before)


def print_batches(label: str, plan: list[dict]) -> None:
    batches: dict[tuple[str, str], int] = defaultdict(int)
    for migration in plan:
        batches[(migration["from"], migration["to"])] += 1
    print(f"\n=== {label}: {len(plan)} keys ({100 * len(plan) / len(KEYS):.1f}%) ===")
    for (source, destination), count in sorted(batches.items(), key=lambda item: -item[1]):
        print(f"  {source} → {destination}: {count}")


def main() -> None:
    add_ring = HashRing()
    add_ring.build(NODES_3)
    add_plan = add_ring.add_node("node-d", KEYS)
    print_batches("add migrations", add_plan)

    remove_ring = HashRing()
    remove_ring.build(NODES_4)
    remove_plan = remove_ring.remove_node("node-d", KEYS)
    print_batches("remove migrations", remove_plan)


if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
```

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import hashlib
import sqlite3
from pathlib import Path

NUM_SHARDS = 8
NUM_BUCKETS = 10


def stable_hash(key: str) -> int:
    return int(hashlib.md5(key.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest(), 16)


def shard_for(key: str, num_shards: int = NUM_SHARDS) -> int:
    return stable_hash(key) % num_shards


def bucket_key(post_id: int, bucket: int) -> str:
    return f"{post_id}#{bucket:02d}"


def shard_path(root: Path, shard: int) -> Path:
    return root / f"shard-{shard}.sqlite3"


def initialize(root: Path) -> None:
    root.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    for shard in range(NUM_SHARDS):
        with sqlite3.connect(shard_path(root, shard)) as db:
            db.execute(
                """
                CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS counters (
                    counter_key TEXT PRIMARY KEY,
                    value INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (value >= 0)
                )
                """
            )


def increment(root: Path, key: str, delta: int = 1) -> int:
    shard = shard_for(key)
    with sqlite3.connect(shard_path(root, shard)) as db:
        db.execute(
            """
            INSERT INTO counters (counter_key, value) VALUES (?, ?)
            ON CONFLICT(counter_key) DO UPDATE SET value = counters.value + excluded.value
            """,
            (key, delta),
        )
        row = db.execute(
            "SELECT value FROM counters WHERE counter_key = ?", (key,)
        ).fetchone()
    return row[0]


def get_count(root: Path, key: str) -> int:
    shard = shard_for(key)
    with sqlite3.connect(shard_path(root, shard)) as db:
        row = db.execute(
            "SELECT value FROM counters WHERE counter_key = ?", (key,)
        ).fetchone()
    return 0 if row is None else row[0]


def delete_counter(root: Path, key: str) -> None:
    shard = shard_for(key)
    with sqlite3.connect(shard_path(root, shard)) as db:
        db.execute("DELETE FROM counters WHERE counter_key = ?", (key,))


def write_plain(root: Path, post_id: int, writes: int) -> dict[int, int]:
    key = str(post_id)
    distribution = {shard: 0 for shard in range(NUM_SHARDS)}
    shard = shard_for(key)
    for _ in range(writes):
        increment(root, key)
        distribution[shard] += 1
    return distribution


def write_split(
    root: Path, post_id: int, writes: int, num_buckets: int = NUM_BUCKETS
) -> dict[int, int]:
    distribution = {shard: 0 for shard in range(NUM_SHARDS)}
    for write_number in range(writes):
        key = bucket_key(post_id, write_number % num_buckets)
        shard = shard_for(key)
        increment(root, key)
        distribution[shard] += 1
    return distribution


def read_fanout(
    root: Path, post_id: int, num_buckets: int = NUM_BUCKETS
) -> dict[str, object]:
    keys = [str(post_id)] + [
        bucket_key(post_id, bucket) for bucket in range(num_buckets)
    ]
    total = 0
    shards_touched = set()
    for key in keys:
        value = get_count(root, key)
        total += value
        if value != 0:
            shards_touched.add(shard_for(key))
    return {"value": total, "shards_touched": sorted(shards_touched)}


def merge_on_cooldown(
    root: Path, post_id: int, num_buckets: int = NUM_BUCKETS
) -> int:
    bucket_keys = [bucket_key(post_id, bucket) for bucket in range(num_buckets)]
    moved = sum(get_count(root, key) for key in bucket_keys)
    if moved:
        increment(root, str(post_id), moved)
    for key in bucket_keys:
        delete_counter(root, key)
    return moved
```

test_hot_key_sqlite.py:
```python
from pathlib import Path
from tempfile import TemporaryDirectory

import ch7_hot_key_sqlite as hot


def nonzero_shards(distribution: dict[int, int]) -> list[int]:
    return [shard for shard, writes in distribution.items() if writes > 0]


with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    hot.initialize(root)
    assert hot.increment(root, "probe") == 1
    assert hot.increment(root, "probe") == 2
    assert hot.get_count(root, "missing") == 0
    hot.delete_counter(root, "missing")
    assert hot.get_count(root, "missing") == 0

    plain = hot.write_plain(root, 9001, 1_000)
    assert set(plain) == set(range(hot.NUM_SHARDS))
    assert sum(plain.values()) == 1_000
    assert len(nonzero_shards(plain)) == 1
    assert hot.get_count(root, "9001") == 1_000
    assert len(list(root.glob("shard-*.sqlite3"))) == hot.NUM_SHARDS

with TemporaryDirectory() as directory:
    root = Path(directory)
    hot.initialize(root)
    split = hot.write_split(root, 9001, 1_000)
    assert set(split) == set(range(hot.NUM_SHARDS))
    assert sum(split.values()) == 1_000
    assert len(nonzero_shards(split)) > 1
    assert max(split.values()) < 1_000

    expected_bucket_shards = sorted(
        {
            hot.shard_for(hot.bucket_key(9001, bucket))
            for bucket in range(hot.NUM_BUCKETS)
        }
    )
    before = hot.read_fanout(root, 9001)
    assert before["value"] == 1_000
    assert before["shards_touched"] == expected_bucket_shards

    assert hot.merge_on_cooldown(root, 9001) == 1_000
    assert hot.get_count(root, "9001") == 1_000
    assert all(
        hot.get_count(root, hot.bucket_key(9001, bucket)) == 0
        for bucket in range(hot.NUM_BUCKETS)
    )
    after = hot.read_fanout(root, 9001)
    assert after == {
        "value": 1_000,
        "shards_touched": [hot.shard_for("9001")],
    }

print("hot-key checks passed")
```

Salted keys have distinct stable hashes, so the application routes their writes to multiple independent SQLite files; SQLite itself is not performing the sharding. Before cooldown, the total is stored across the bucket counters, so a read must fan out and sum all relevant keys. A production merge would need coordination such as pausing/rerouting writes, idempotent merge state, and recovery or distributed-workflow handling because updates and deletes span independent shard transactions.

Run evidence:
```text
$ python3 test_hot_key_sqlite.py
hot-key checks passed
```

practice.task: [PostgreSQL, Citus] Learn how to colocate schema-based tenant tables.
practice.question:
A B2B helpdesk SaaS keeps each tenant's `tickets` and `comments` tables in a separate PostgreSQL schema. In this lab, you will use Citus schema-based sharding so every tenant schema becomes its own colocated placement unit.

Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop).

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch7-p5 init
docker compose up -d
```

:::cut Inspect the starter files and schema
Run:

```bash
ls -l
```

Expected lab files: `docker-compose.yml`, `setup.sql`, and `test.sql`. The compose file defines a Citus coordinator and two workers. The starter `setup.sql` creates two tenant schemas and leaves the schema-distribution step incomplete:

```sql
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS acme CASCADE;
DROP SCHEMA IF EXISTS globex CASCADE;

CREATE SCHEMA acme;
CREATE SCHEMA globex;

CREATE TABLE acme.tickets (
  ticket_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  title text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE acme.comments (
  comment_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES acme.tickets(ticket_id),
  body text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE globex.tickets (
  ticket_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  title text NOT NULL
);
CREATE TABLE globex.comments (
  comment_id bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  ticket_id bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES globex.tickets(ticket_id),
  body text NOT NULL
);

-- TODO: distribute both tenant schemas after their tables exist.

SELECT table_name, citus_table_type, colocation_id, nodename
FROM citus_shards
WHERE table_name::text LIKE 'acme.%'
   OR table_name::text LIKE 'globex.%'
ORDER BY table_name::text;
```
:::

Tasks:

1. Wait for the Citus extension on all three nodes, then register the coordinator and both workers with the native Citus node-management functions:

   ```bash
   for service in coordinator worker1 worker2; do
     until docker compose exec -T "$service" psql -U postgres -tAc \
       "SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname = 'citus'" | grep -q 1; do
       sleep 2
     done
   done

   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres <<'SQL'
   SELECT citus_set_coordinator_host('coordinator', 5432);
   SELECT citus_add_node('worker1', 5432)
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_dist_node WHERE nodename = 'worker1');
   SELECT citus_add_node('worker2', 5432)
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_dist_node WHERE nodename = 'worker2');
   SQL
   ```

2. Complete the placeholder in `setup.sql`. After all tables exist, call `citus_schema_distribute` once for `acme` and once for `globex`. Each schema's tables must share one colocation ID and worker placement, while the two tenant schemas must have distinct colocation IDs.

3. Apply the completed schema through the coordinator:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres < setup.sql
   ```

4. Run the tests:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres < test.sql
   ```

   The success signal is `schema sharding checks passed`.

5. In 3-4 sentences, explain why schema-based sharding preserves joins and foreign keys within one tenant schema, and when shared row-based tables distributed by `tenant_id` would be preferable.

6. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.

practice.task: [PostgreSQL, Citus] Learn how to colocate tenant data for single-shard joins.
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Desktop, or Docker Engine 24+ with the Docker Compose v2 plugin installed.

This lab uses a three-node Citus cluster to hash-shard a project-management SaaS by `tenant_id` and colocate each tenant's related rows for single-shard joins.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch7-p6 init
docker compose up -d
```

:::cut Inspect the starter files
Run:

```bash
ls -l
```

Expected lab files: `docker-compose.yml`, `setup.sql`, and `test.sql`, plus `preloaded_data/seed.sql`. The compose stack loads the fixed table schema and project fixture from that seed file when the coordinator is initialized. The starter `setup.sql` contains only the two edit sites for the distribution and constraint work:

```sql
-- implement: reference table and tenant distribution
DO $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE 'distribution not implemented'; END $$;

-- implement: tenant-aware keys and foreign keys
DO $$ BEGIN RAISE NOTICE 'constraints not implemented'; END $$;
```
:::

Tasks:

1. Poll all three nodes only to confirm that the Citus extension is ready. Then use the single `psql` session shown below, connected to `coordinator`, to run `citus_set_coordinator_host` and both guarded `citus_add_node` calls. Do not run those registration functions on either worker:

   ```bash
   for s in coordinator worker1 worker2; do
     until docker compose exec -T "$s" psql -U postgres -tAc \
       "SELECT 1 FROM pg_extension WHERE extname='citus'" | grep -q 1; do
       sleep 2
     done
   done

   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres <<'SQL'
   SELECT citus_set_coordinator_host('coordinator', 5432);
   SELECT citus_add_node('worker1', 5432)
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_dist_node WHERE nodename = 'worker1');
   SELECT citus_add_node('worker2', 5432)
   WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM pg_dist_node WHERE nodename = 'worker2');
   SQL
   ```

2. In the first placeholder block, make `plans` a reference table, set the session's `citus.shard_count` to 8, distribute `tenants` by `tenant_id`, and colocate `projects` and `tasks` with `tenants`.

3. In the second placeholder block, add the exact ordered primary keys `tenants (tenant_id)`, `projects (tenant_id, project_id)`, and `tasks (tenant_id, task_id)`, so the `tenant_id` prefix aligns each distributed key with Citus routing. Add foreign keys for tenant-plan, project-tenant, and task-project relationships. Include `tenant_id` on both sides of foreign keys between distributed tables; the tenant-plan foreign key may reference the `plans` reference table by `plan_code`. Add each constraint with a separate `ALTER TABLE` statement because Citus rejects an `ADD CONSTRAINT` command combined with other subcommands.

4. Apply the completed file to the preloaded tables:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres < setup.sql
   ```

5. Run the tests:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec -T coordinator psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres < test.sql
   ```

6. Optionally inspect the metadata and the executed join plan in an interactive coordinator session:

   ```bash
   docker compose exec coordinator psql -U postgres
   ```

   Use `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, COSTS OFF)` when you want the plan to report work that was actually executed.

7. Explain in 2-3 sentences why tenant-owned joins and distributed-table keys carry `tenant_id`.

8. Tear down the Docker stack with `docker compose down -v`.

practice.task: [PostgreSQL] Learn how row-level security isolates tenants
practice.question:
Prerequisites: Docker Engine 24+ (or Docker Desktop). No local PostgreSQL installation is required.

This lab uses PostgreSQL 16 with a preloaded shared-table SaaS schema. You will add row-level security, least-privilege roles, and transaction-local tenant context.

Setup:

```bash
docker run --rm -v "$PWD:/out" ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch7-p7 init
docker run -d --name lab-ch7-p7 -p 5432:5432 ghcr.io/anmisttt/lab:ch7-p7
```

:::cut Inspect the starter and preloaded schema
The image initializes the database from `seed.sql`. The `init` command exposes that source as `preloaded_data/seed.sql` for inspection and copies the incomplete `setup.sql` and supplied `test.sql`.

```bash
ls -l setup.sql test.sql preloaded_data/seed.sql
sed -n '1,200p' preloaded_data/seed.sql
docker exec -i lab-ch7-p7 psql -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab <<'SQL'
SELECT
  array_agg(name ORDER BY name) AS visible_projects,
  count(DISTINCT tenant_id) AS visible_tenants
FROM rls_lab.projects;
SQL
```

Expected lab files: `setup.sql`, `test.sql`, and `preloaded_data/seed.sql`.

The baseline query reports both Alpha project and Beta project across two tenants. The incomplete `setup.sql` is the student authorization script; it does not recreate the schema or seed rows.
:::

Tasks:

1. Run the inspection commands above. Confirm that the administrator can see both tenants before row-level security is configured.

2. Complete `setup.sql` with a non-login role that owns the existing `rls_lab` schema, `projects` table, and identity sequence, plus a separate login role for application queries. The application role must not own those objects, be a member of the owner role, or have `SUPERUSER`, `BYPASSRLS`, `CREATEROLE`, `CREATEDB`, or `REPLICATION`. Make the authorization script safe to run repeatedly while preserving the preloaded schema and rows.

3. Grant the application role only `USAGE` on the schema; `SELECT`, `INSERT`, `UPDATE`, and `DELETE` on `projects`; and `USAGE` on its identity sequence. Do not grant schema creation, object ownership, policy-management privileges, `SELECT` or `UPDATE` on the identity sequence, or `MAINTAIN`, `TRUNCATE`, `REFERENCES`, or `TRIGGER` on the table.

4. Enable and force row-level security on `rls_lab.projects`. Create a policy for the application role whose `USING` and `WITH CHECK` expressions compare the row's `tenant_id` with `NULLIF(current_setting('app.tenant_id', true), '')::uuid`. Explain which operations `USING` controls and which new row values `WITH CHECK` validates.

5. Apply the completed authorization script:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch7-p7 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab < setup.sql
   ```

6. Open an application-role session through the administrator connection with `SET ROLE`. Inside an explicit transaction, set tenant A with transaction-local `set_config(..., true)`, confirm an unfiltered query returns only Alpha project, and attempt to insert a tenant B row. Confirm PostgreSQL rejects the insert with a row-level security policy error. Because the error aborts the transaction, issue `ROLLBACK` before continuing to Task 7.

   ```bash
   docker exec -it lab-ch7-p7 psql -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab
   ```

7. In explicit transactions, inspect `current_user`, `session_user`, `rolsuper`, and `rolbypassrls`. Confirm that the application role sees no rows without tenant context, the table owner is subject to default-deny under `FORCE ROW LEVEL SECURITY` because it has no applicable policy, and the administrator still sees both rows. Commit a transaction that set tenant A locally, then verify that the setting is cleared and the application role again sees no rows. Explain the implications for GUI-client auto-commit, pooled connections, and deriving tenant identity from verified authentication.

8. Prove the authorization script is repeatable by applying `setup.sql` a second time with error-stop enabled, then run the supplied checks:

   ```bash
   docker exec -i lab-ch7-p7 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab < setup.sql
   docker exec -i lab-ch7-p7 psql -v ON_ERROR_STOP=1 -U postgres -d ch7_rls_lab < test.sql
   ```

   Success is signaled by `RLS checks passed`.

9. Tear down the Docker lab with `docker rm -f lab-ch7-p7`.
